name: Sandboxing and Egress Control
question: If the agent runs code, what can that code touch?
summary: Code written by a model, especially after reading untrusted content, must be treated as hostile. Run it in an isolated sandbox, such as a gVisor container or a Firecracker microVM, with no host secrets or mounts, CPU, memory and time limits, short-lived scoped credentials, and network access only through an egress proxy with an allowlist. Then a successful injection can only reach what the sandbox allows.
useCases: Coding agents that run tests, installs or scripts

no host environment variables; short-lived tokens scoped to one task
none, or an egress proxy with a domain allowlist
CPU, memory, disk and wall-clock time
a fresh sandbox per task, destroyed afterwards
no host mounts; read-only inputs, write-only outputs

steps.title: A fresh sandbox per task
steps.text: Every task gets a new working directory and a new container. Nothing written by one task survives to the next.

steps.title: Isolate the kernel
steps.text: The gVisor runtime, runsc, intercepts system calls in a user-space kernel, so code that tries a kernel exploit hits gVisor instead of the host. A microVM would isolate further.

steps.title: Cut the network
steps.text: network_mode none means injected code has no way to send data out. If installs are needed, route them through a proxy that allows only your package mirror.

steps.title: Limit resources
steps.text: 256 MB of memory, one CPU, 64 processes and a 30-second timeout stop crypto-mining and fork bombs.

steps.title: No secrets, no writes
steps.text: An empty environment, all capabilities dropped, an unprivileged user and read-only mounts: there is nothing to steal and nowhere to hide.

steps.title: Destroy it afterwards
steps.text: remove=True deletes the container when the task ends, so an attacker cannot leave anything behind for later.

practice.scenario: A fintech’s spending-analysis assistant writes Python to chart a customer’s transactions. The code used to run inside the API container, next to the service’s database credentials. Now each task runs in a fresh gVisor container with no network, 256 MB of memory, one CPU, a 30-second limit and only the transaction file mounted read-only.

industries.use: Run model-written analysis code on transaction files in isolation
Execute student and model code in a coding tutor without host access
Let an analytics agent run SQL and Python against a copy, never production

practice.analogy: A bomb-disposal box. You assume what is inside might go off, so it is opened only where it cannot hurt anything else.

library.name: Docker SDK for Python + gVisor
library.what: Start a throwaway container per task with gVisor’s runsc runtime, no network and strict limits.

practice.note: If the code must install packages, route it through an egress proxy that allows only your package mirror instead of opening the network.

samples.code:
import docker, pathlib, tempfile

client = docker.from_env()

def run_untrusted(code: str, data_file: str) -> str:
    work = pathlib.Path(tempfile.mkdtemp())
    (work / "task.py").write_text(code)
    return client.containers.run(
        "python:3.12-slim", ["timeout", "30", "python", "/work/task.py"],
        runtime="runsc",                    # gVisor: a user-space kernel
        network_mode="none",                # no network at all
        mem_limit="256m", nano_cpus=1_000_000_000, pids_limit=64,
        read_only=True, cap_drop=["ALL"], user="65534:65534",
        environment={},                     # no host secrets
        volumes={str(work): {"bind": "/work", "mode": "ro"},
                 data_file: {"bind": "/data/tx.csv", "mode": "ro"}},
        remove=True, stdout=True, stderr=True,
    ).decode()

numericDrill.question: Code tasks in your sandbox make 2,000 outbound requests in a day. 1,950 go to your package mirror, which the egress proxy allows; the rest go elsewhere and are blocked. What share of requests is blocked, in percent?
numericDrill.answer: 50 ÷ 2,000 = 2.5%. Each blocked request is worth reviewing: some are harmless, such as telemetry, but some may be injected code trying to send data out.

interview.question: Why is a plain container not always enough for untrusted code?
interview.answer: Containers share the host kernel, so a kernel vulnerability can let code escape. gVisor puts a user-space kernel in between, and a microVM such as Firecracker gives the code its own kernel, which is a much stronger boundary. The choice depends on how hostile the code may be.

interview.question: What should a sandbox for agent code never contain?
interview.answer: Host secrets such as environment variables and credential files, host file-system mounts other than the specific inputs, and open network access. Give it a short-lived token scoped to the task, if any, and route network traffic through an allowlisting proxy.

mistakes.mistake: Running generated code in the application container
mistakes.fix: Use a fresh, isolated sandbox per task

mistakes.mistake: Opening the network so package installs work
mistakes.fix: Allow only your package mirror through an egress proxy

quiz.question: Where should model-written analysis code run?
options: In an isolated sandbox with no host secrets
quiz.explanation: Treat generated code as hostile and isolate it.

quiz.question: Why is a plain container a weaker boundary than a microVM?
options: Containers share the host kernel, so a kernel exploit can escape
quiz.explanation: MicroVMs give code its own kernel.

quiz.question: What does gVisor’s runsc runtime do?
options: Handles system calls in a user-space kernel, shielding the host kernel
quiz.explanation: gVisor narrows the host attack surface.

quiz.question: Of 2,000 outbound requests from sandboxed code, 1,950 go to the package mirror (allowed) and the rest are blocked. What share is blocked?
Which should never be passed into a sandbox for untrusted code? Select all that apply.
options: A read-only copy of the input file
A 15-minute token scoped to one task
quiz.explanation: Host secrets and long-lived keys must stay out; scoped inputs are fine.

quiz.question: Package installs fail because the sandbox has no network. What is the best fix?
options: Route traffic through an egress proxy that allows only the package mirror
quiz.explanation: Allow narrowly instead of opening everything.

quiz.question: Hostile code starts a crypto miner inside the sandbox. What stops it?
Why destroy the sandbox after each task?
options: So nothing an attacker leaves behind survives to a later task

quiz.question: Which settings harden a Docker-run sandbox? Select all that apply.
options: network_mode none, or an egress proxy
cap_drop ALL and an unprivileged user
Mounting the host’s home directory read-write
Passing the Docker socket into the container
quiz.explanation: Removing network, capabilities and privileges helps; host mounts and the Docker socket give escape routes.

quiz.question: A browser agent runs in a sandbox with open internet. Which risk remains largest?
options: Visited pages injecting instructions and data leaving through the browser
quiz.explanation: Browsing is untrusted input and an outbound channel at once.

quiz.question: Which isolation is strongest for actively hostile code?
quiz.explanation: A microVM has its own kernel behind a hypervisor.

quiz.question: An analytics agent needs to query data. Which designs are safer? Select all that apply.
options: Query a read-only replica or copy, never production
Use a short-lived credential scoped to that dataset
Allow any SQL, including writes, on production

quiz.question: Which ASI entry covers an agent or sandbox boundary failing so that arbitrary code runs?
Which hosted service offers sandboxes built for AI-generated code?
quiz.explanation: E2B provides isolated sandboxes for model-written code.

quiz.question: A code sandbox must install packages and call one internal API. Which configuration fits? Select all that apply.
options: An egress proxy allowing only the package mirror and that API
A scoped, short-lived token for the API
quiz.explanation: Narrow egress plus a scoped token keeps both tasks working safely.

quiz.question: Why mount inputs read-only?
options: Hostile code cannot tamper with or plant files in the inputs

quiz.question: What is the main risk of running generated code in the application’s own container?
options: The code can read the service’s secrets and reach everything the service can
quiz.explanation: It inherits every privilege of the application.

quiz.question: Which are typical resource limits for a code sandbox? Select all that apply.
quiz.explanation: Time and memory caps, plus process and disk limits, contain abuse.

quiz.question: Which statement is correct about sandboxing and prompt injection?
options: Sandboxing limits what injected code can reach, but does not stop the injection itself
Sandboxing only matters without a system prompt
quiz.explanation: It contains damage; other layers prevent the steering.

quiz.question: A red-team test shows sandboxed code can still reach an attacker’s server. Which fixes apply? Select all that apply.
options: Route all traffic through an allowlisting proxy
Block direct outbound connections at the network layer
quiz.explanation: Egress must be forced through the allowlist.
